client: I've been really struggling lately with all these medical bills that piled up after my surgery, and honestly it's been keeping me up at night. Every time I check my bank account or the mail, I feel this wave of panic that just doesn't go away. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change the actual numbers, but I guess I'm here because I don't know what else to do.
therapist:
It takes real courage to reach out even when things feel overwhelming, and I want you to know that what you're feeling — that wave of panic — makes complete sense given the pressure you're carrying right now. You're right that our conversation won't change the numbers on those bills, but it can help us understand what's happening in your mind when you check that mail, because often the *anticipation* and the stories we tell ourselves can amplify the fear beyond what's already hard enough. 

I'm curious — when that wave of panic hits, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in that moment?

client: When I open the mailbox and see something official-looking, my mind immediately jumps to "this is it, this is the one that finally breaks everything." It's like I'm already picturing myself losing my apartment, telling my family I failed, all of that in about two seconds flat. I know it sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but in that moment it feels completely real and inevitable.
therapist:
It doesn't sound dramatic at all — your mind is trying to protect you by scanning for the worst possible outcome, and that's actually a very human response to prolonged stress. What you're describing is something we call "catastrophizing," where our thoughts leap from one difficult moment all the way to the worst-case ending, skipping over all the steps and possibilities in between. 

I'm wondering — when you think back on difficult situations you've faced before, have there been times where your mind predicted "this is the one that breaks everything," and yet you found a way through that you couldn't have anticipated in that panicked moment?

client: I mean... yeah, I guess there have been times like that. I remember when I thought I was going to get fired about two years ago after making a big mistake at work, and I spent weeks convinced it was over, but it actually ended up being okay. But I don't know, this situation with my job feels different somehow — like my gut is telling me this time it really is as bad as I think it is.
therapist:
That memory you just shared is really important — it shows that you have genuine evidence of your own resilience, that past-you survived something that felt just as certain and final as this feels now. It's worth gently noticing that your gut gave you a very similar warning signal two years ago, and while that feeling was real and valid, it turned out not to be a reliable predictor of the actual outcome. 

What do you think might be different about this situation that makes it feel more certain to you — is it the specific facts of it, or could it be that the fear itself feels more intense after everything your body and mind have been through with the surgery?

client: I mean... I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to accept that, but it's hard not to feel like this time is actually different. After the surgery, my body just isn't the same, my stamina is lower, and I've missed so much at work that I genuinely don't know if my manager still trusts me. It's not just a feeling — there are real things that have changed, and I'm scared that what I survived before doesn't count for much when the circumstances are so different now.
therapist:
You're making a really fair and grounded point — this isn't pure catastrophizing, there are real changes in your body and your work situation, and it wouldn't be helpful for me to dismiss those as just anxious thinking. What I'd gently invite you to consider is whether there might be a middle ground between "my past resilience doesn't count" and "everything is fine," because the skills and resourcefulness that got you through before didn't disappear — they're still part of you, even if the circumstances have shifted. 

What would it look like to take one small, concrete step this week — maybe a conversation with your manager or looking into a payment plan for the bills — that could give you some actual information rather than leaving your mind to fill in the blanks on its own?

client: I hear what you're saying about the middle ground, and part of me wants to believe that my past resilience is still in there somewhere. But when you mention talking to my manager, that actually makes my stomach drop — I've been avoiding that conversation because I'm terrified she's going to confirm my worst fears about my performance slipping. It feels safer to just not know, even though I realize that probably sounds counterproductive.
therapist:
It doesn't sound counterproductive at all — it sounds very human, because avoiding something that feels threatening is our mind's way of protecting us from pain in the short term, even when it keeps us stuck in the long term. What's worth noticing is that right now, your mind is filling that unknown space with your worst fears as if they're already confirmed facts, so in a way, you're already living with the painful outcome without any of the actual information. 

What do you imagine might happen inside you — not with your manager, but within yourself — if you heard something difficult from her versus continuing to carry this uncertainty indefinitely?

client: That's... actually a really uncomfortable question to sit with, because I think part of me knows the answer already. If I heard something difficult from her, at least I'd know — there'd be something concrete to deal with, even if it hurt. But carrying this uncertainty is like this constant low hum of dread that never lets me rest, and I'm starting to wonder if I've been choosing the hum because it feels safer than a single loud crash.
therapist:
That insight you just named — choosing the constant hum over the risk of a single crash — is genuinely profound, and it tells me that a wise part of you already understands what's been keeping you stuck. There's real courage in recognizing that the "safer" choice has actually been costing you sleep, peace, and energy every single day, and that the thing you're avoiding might actually be more survivable than the endless waiting. 

I'm wondering — what would it feel like to treat that conversation with your manager not as a verdict on your worth, but as simply gathering information that lets you finally start dealing with reality instead of your fears about it?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me really wants to believe it could feel that simple — just gathering information, not a verdict. But honestly, when I imagine actually sitting across from my manager and asking whether my job is secure, my whole chest tightens up because it doesn't feel neutral at all. What if the information I gather confirms the worst, and then I can't pretend anymore that everything might be okay?
therapist:
That fear you're describing — losing the last bit of hope that things *might* be okay — is one of the most tender and honest things you've shared, and it makes complete sense that you'd want to protect that fragile "maybe." But I want to gently reflect something back to you: the "maybe everything is okay" you're protecting right now is living alongside constant dread, lost sleep, and a chest that tightens every time you check the mail, so it's not really giving you peace — it's just postponing a reality you'd finally have the power to respond to. 

If the conversation did confirm something difficult, what's one resource, person, or strength you could imagine leaning on — even a small one — that tells you you wouldn't have to face that alone?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right that the "maybe" isn't actually giving me peace. But when you ask about who I'd lean on... that's where it gets really hard, because honestly, I don't have a clear answer, and that scares me almost as much as the financial situation itself. I have one friend I might call, but I'd feel so guilty burdening her, and I'm not sure she'd really get it anyway.
therapist:
The fact that one person came to mind at all matters more than you might realize right now, and that instinct to reach out — even if it feels complicated — is worth paying attention to. I'd gently ask you to notice that the story "I'd be a burden" is another thought, not a confirmed fact, and it might be worth examining the same way we looked at your fears about your manager — because people who care about us often *want* to show up, even imperfectly. 

What do you think your friend would actually say if she knew you were carrying all of this alone — the bills, the surgery recovery, the work anxiety — and that you'd been protecting her from it?

client: Honestly, if I really think about what she'd say... she'd probably be upset that I didn't tell her sooner. She's that kind of person, you know, she'd want to know. But then there's this other voice that says maybe I'm just telling myself that because it's what I want to believe, not because it's actually true.
therapist:
That "other voice" that questions your own hopeful thoughts is worth noticing — it's working very hard to protect you from disappointment, but it's also systematically dismantling every potential source of support before you even give it a chance. What's striking is that you described her with real specificity — "she's that kind of person" — which suggests this isn't just wishful thinking, but something you actually know about her from experience. 

What would it mean for you to treat reaching out to her as a small experiment — not a guarantee, but a chance to test what you actually know about her against what your fear is predicting?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually likes the idea of framing it as an experiment — it feels less all-or-nothing that way. But I think what scares me is that even if I reach out and she responds warmly, that other voice will just find a way to explain it away, like "she was just being polite" or "she felt obligated." It's like the fear has a backup plan for every outcome, so I'm not sure the experiment can ever really give me the answer I need.
therapist:
You've just identified something really important — that this protective voice has built an unfalsifiable fortress where no positive outcome can ever count as real evidence, and that's exhausting because it means you've been playing a game where the rules are rigged against you finding any comfort. This is actually really valuable to see clearly, because when we notice that a thought pattern rejects *all* evidence to the contrary, that's a sign it's driven by fear rather than reality. 

What do you think it would take — even just a little — to let one warm response from her land as real and true, rather than handing it straight over to that other voice to explain away?
